<x_0.0977><y_0.0305>Execution a criminal, fo reviving, was not allowed to take func-
tuary and abjure the realm; but his fleeing to fanétuary
was held an escape in the officer.<x_0.9844><y_0.0703><class_Text>

<x_0.2607><y_0.0695>EXECUTION, in the law of Scotland. See LAW Index.<x_0.9814><y_0.0852><class_Text>

<x_0.2197><y_0.0844>EXECUTION, in the French mufic, is ufed to denote
the manner of finging, or of the performance of a fong.
" As to the manner of finging, called in France _execu-_
tion, no nation may, with any probability dispute it
with the French. If the French, by their commerce
with the Italians have gained a bolder composition,
the Italians have made their advantage of the French,
in learning of them a more polite, moving, and exqui-
fite execution." St Evremond.<x_0.9824><y_0.2039><class_Text>

<x_0.2188><y_0.2047>EXECUTIVE POWER. The fupreme executive
power of thefe kingdoms is veffed by our laws in a
fingle perfon, the king or queen for the time being.
See the article KING.<x_0.9834><y_0.2586><class_Text>

<x_0.2168><y_0.2578>The executive power, in this flate, hath a right to
a negative in parliament, i. e. to refute affent to any
acts offered; otherwise the two other branches of legi-
lative power would, or might, become defpotic.<x_0.9805><y_0.3125><class_Text>

<x_0.2158><y_0.3117>EXECUTOR, a perfon nominated by a teflator, to
take care to fee his will and teflament executed or per-
formed, and his effects difpofed of according to the te-
nor of the will. See LAW.<x_0.9795><y_0.3648><class_Text>

<x_0.2148><y_0.3656>EXECUTOR, in _Scots Law_, fignifies either the perfon
entitled to fuceed to the moveable elate of one deceafed,
or who by law or fpecial appointment is intrufted with
the administration of it.<x_0.9785><y_0.4188><class_Text>

<x_0.2139><y_0.4195>EXECUTORY, in _Law_, is where an elitate in fee,
that is, made by deed or fine, is to be executed after-
wards by entry, livery, or writ. Leafe for years, an-
nuities, conditions, &c. are termed _inheritances exec-_
_cutory._<x_0.9775><y_0.4859><class_Text>

<x_0.2129><y_0.4852>EXECUTRY, in _Scots Law_, is the moveable elate
failing to the executor. Under executry, or moveables,
is comprehended every thing that moves itself, or can
be moved; fuch as corns, cattle, furniture, ready mo-
ney, &c.<x_0.9766><y_0.5539><class_Text>

<x_0.2119><y_0.5523>EXEDRÆ, in antiquity, denoted halls with many
feats, where the philofophers, rhetoricians, and men of
learning, met for discourte and difputation. The word
occurs in ecclesiailical writers as a general name for
fuch buildings as were diltinet from the main body of
the churches, and yet within the limits of the church
taken in its largeft fenfe. Among the exedre the chief
was the BAPTISTERY.<x_0.9756><y_0.6609><class_Text>

<x_0.2109><y_0.6602>EXEGESIS, a difcourte by way of explanation or
comment upon any subject. In the Scotch universities,
there is an exercile among the students in divinity, call-
ed an _exegelfs_, in which a question is fitted by the re-
fpondent, who is then oppofed by two or three other
fludents in their turns; during which time the profef-
for moderates, and felves the difficulties which the re-
fpondent cannot overcome.<x_0.9746><y_0.7688><class_Text>

<x_0.21><y_0.7664>EXEGETES, (formed of _Enyieμai_, "I explain,")
among the Athenians, perfons learned in the laws,
whom the judges ufed to confult in capital caufes.<x_0.9736><y_0.8086><class_Text>

<x_0.209><y_0.807>EXEGETICA, in _Algebra_, the art of finding, ei-
ther in numbers or lines, the roots of the equation of a
problem, according as the problem is either numerical
or geometrical.<x_0.9727><y_0.8625><class_Text>

<x_0.208><y_0.8609>EXEMPLAR, a model, or original, to be imitated,
or copied. See MODEL.<x_0.9717><y_0.8898><class_Text>

<x_0.2461><y_0.8875>EXEMPLAR alfo denotes the idea, or image, conceived<x_0.9707><y_0.9055><class_Text>
